chapter: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
title: Eckstine gives up the big band and offers him $100 a week
summary: With the war over and debts of about $25,000, Eckstine goes solo and asks Malachi to be his pianist and musical director.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: It was around late summer of 1947 that Billy Eckstine finally gave up his band, because the War was over and all the principal guys had left. And he had good men in his band. He had acquired tenor saxophonist Frank Wess. By this time Miles Davis was in New York, and he had Miles Davis in the band. He had Kenny Dorham in the band on trumpet. And Norris Turner [SIC: NORRIS TURNEY?], the alto saxophone player. I was trying to think of his name the other day, who played with the band. He was from Cincinnati. Norris Turner (sic), a very, very good alto saxophone player. He had a good band, and good people in the band. But the original spark seemed to have died out, along with the fact that it was post-war and there were a lot of musicians back, and the economy was up, salaries were big and everything, and he was going more and more in debt.

So he came through Washington, and he played a club on U Street called the Bengassi(?). He was doing a single in there. He called me and asked me if I would come up to the Bengassi and do this week with him there. During that time, I

think the trio wasn't working, or we had just disbanded or something. Anyway, I went up and did this week with him. And while I was there, he was telling me that he owed the agents in New York...I think he owed something like $25,000. He was telling me that he'd gone into debt, and he just couldn't handle the band, he couldn't keep the band any longer. He said he was going to do a single, and he would be happy to have me as his pianist and musical director or whatever. But I think he told me he could only pay me $100 a week, but he'd try to get... I think it was probably one of his first dates as a single. He said that his agent, a guy named Milt, Milt Something, I can't remember his name... His manager had some work lined up for him, and he was sure that in no time he'd be able to pay me a better salary.

Well, $100 a week wasn't good money under any standards, you know. But it was a thing where I could eke out a couple of dollars to send home to my family, and find some cheap place to live. Anyway, I decided I'd go with him. I think another main attraction was that we were going back to 52nd Street, and we were going for an extended engagement there. So I felt like if I went back to New York, while I was there perhaps some other things could happen.
